body:
## The query shape

A correlated `EXISTS` (or correlated `IN`) whose subquery also carries a predicate on the outer key only:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.customer_id > 17000);
```

This is what query generators and hand-written reports produce when a restriction on the outer row is written next to the correlation instead of in the outer `WHERE`: the two places are equivalent for `EXISTS`, and a view or a template often only allows adding conditions inside the subquery. Written in the outer `WHERE`, the predicate is pushed into the scan of `orders`. Written inside the subquery it is not: the outer rows are produced in full and the predicate is only applied to the duplicate-eliminated domain.

## What happens today

The subquery is decorrelated into a materialized CTE of the outer rows with two references: the outer rows on the left side of a MARK join, and the domain of distinct keys below the subquery. The predicate `o.customer_id > 17000` ends up as a filter on the domain reference only. The CTE filter pusher restricts a CTE only when every reference is filtered, so the scan of `orders` stays unfiltered:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]                                ~3,000,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      CTE_SCAN                                                          ~3,000,000 rows
      ... HASH_JOIN INNER customer_id = customer_id
            (GROUP BY over FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000) over CTE_SCAN)
            SEQ_SCAN customers  Filters: customer_id > 17000
```

## The change

The change lives in the CTE filter pusher. Before it pushes the filters of the references into a CTE, it treats a join that keeps only the matching rows of a CTE reference as one more consumer filter of that reference:

```
SEMI[l = r](CTE_REF c, R)                 ->  SEMI[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R)
FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](CTE_REF c, R))   ->  FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R))
                                              when p(r) is TRUE for every row of R
```

A left row survives a SEMI join, or a MARK join under a filter on the bare mark, only together with a right row whose key equals its own. A comparison with constants that is TRUE for the key of every right row is therefore TRUE for the key of every surviving left row, and filtering the left side by it first removes only rows that the join drops anyway. With the filter on the outer rows' reference every reference of the CTE is filtered, and the pusher moves the predicate into the CTE definition as it does for any other consumer filter:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]  Filters: customer_id > 17000  ~600,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000)
        CTE_SCAN
      ... (unchanged)
```

It is built from three parts:

- **Orchestration: `CTEFilterPusher::GenerateSemiJoinFilters`**, called from `CTEFilterPusher::Optimize` right after it has collected the CTEs and their references (implemented in `src/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.cpp`). It uses the pusher's own reference inventory to decide whether a reference qualifies (every other reference of the CTE is filtered already) and records the new filter there, so the push that follows sees an ordinary filtered reference. It is part of the `cte_filter_pusher` optimizer and is switched off with it.
- **Discovery: which filters hold for every right row.** A small search follows the right join key down through filters, table filters of a scan, column-reference projections, the groups of an aggregate, the preserved side of joins and the equalities of INNER joins, and collects the filters that compare that column with constants. It does not look at the left side and does not rewrite anything. The positive-MARK case is a separate check (`FILTER` with the bare mark as a conjunct over a MARK comparison join) that only selects the join.
- **Transfer: `FilterCombiner::GenerateJoinFilters`**, unchanged, the helper that `FilterPullup::PullupSemiJoin` and `FilterPushdown::PushdownSemiAntiJoin` use. It derives the left-side filters from the collected right-side filters and the join conditions; the search also uses it for the equalities of an INNER join. Which predicates can cross an equality is therefore decided in one place: comparisons with constants, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists (as `FilterCombiner::GetComparedExpression` defines them). Predicates the helper does not derive (`OR`, `IS [NOT] NULL`, `NOT IN`) are not transferred.

`CTEFilterPusher::PushFilterIntoCTE` is unchanged. It restricts a CTE by the disjunction of the filters of its references and hands that to the expression rewriter, whose `DistributivityRule` reduces `(A AND B) OR A` to `A`. The new filter usually repeats the filter of the other reference, so it is added to the plan as one flat conjunction, which is the form the rule reduces; the scan then gets `customer_id > 17000` and not a disjunction. Nothing else simplifies the pushed filter, for any CTE.

## Preconditions

- The left child of the join is a reference of a materialized CTE (bare or under a filter), not a recurring or correlated reference, and every other reference of that CTE is already filtered. The new filter is then exactly what the CTE filter pusher was missing. Other left sides (for example a plain table scan under an uncorrelated `IN`) are left alone.
- A SEMI comparison join, or a MARK comparison join directly under a filter that has the bare mark as a conjunct. Not ANTI, outer, delim or AsOf joins, and not a mark that is used in any other way (`NOT mark`, under an `OR`, in the select list).
- The join condition is `=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, with a bare column on the right side.
- Only filters that compare the key with constants and cannot throw are transferred: comparisons, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists. A function of the key, an `OR`, a NULL test and `NOT IN` are not.
- "Every right row passes it" is established conservatively: the NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, set operations, CTE references and optional scan filters end the search.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS order_id, (i * 7919) % 20000 AS customer_id, DATE '2024-01-01' + (i % 365)::INTEGER AS order_date,
           ((i % 1000) / 10.0)::DECIMAL(10,1) AS amount, 'note ' || (i % 100000) AS note,
           i % 7 AS status, i % 13 AS channel, i % 101 AS store_id
    FROM range(30000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT i AS customer_id, 'customer ' || i AS name, i % 50 AS region FROM range(18000) t(i);

SELECT status, channel, count(*), sum(amount), max(note), min(order_date), max(store_id)
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND <predicate on o.customer_id>)
GROUP BY status, channel;
```

Base of this branch against the branch, release builds. User-mode instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3, including the 0.24 G of process start-up):

| predicate inside the subquery | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `o.customer_id > 17000` (15 % of the rows pass it, 5 % have a match) | 13.5 G | 5.8 G |
| `o.customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 300 AND c.region < 25` | 13.1 G | 4.2 G |
| `o.customer_id > 100000` (no row can match) | 9.4 G | 0.26 G |
| control: `o.customer_id > 17000` written in the outer `WHERE` | 4.5 G | 4.5 G |

The control shows what is left on the table: with the predicate in the outer `WHERE` the subquery is deliminated into a plain semi join. The change does not rewrite the query into that form, it only stops the scan from producing rows that cannot match.

## Regression check

None of the TPC-H and TPC-DS queries has this shape, so the two suites are regression evidence only and the example above carries the case. Base against branch at SF1:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change;
- results with 1 and with 16 threads: identical (one query differs in the last digit of a floating-point aggregate between two parallel runs of the same binary);
- `scripts/plan_cost_runner.py` on `benchmark/tpch_plan_cost`: no differences.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.test` (434 assertions): 42 result cases over tables with NULL, duplicate and unmatched keys on both sides (empty left / right side, null-safe correlation, `NOT EXISTS`, `EXISTS` as a value, the mark under an `OR`, a predicate that can throw, the NULL-extended side of a LEFT join, grouping sets, `UNION`, nested `EXISTS`, correlated `IN`, VARCHAR and DATE keys, DOUBLE keys with `0.0`, `-0.0` and NaN, references of a materialized CTE whose filters differ only in the sign of a zero passed to `signbit`, query-written materialized CTEs with one reference, a reference that is filtered already, two filtered references and one unfiltered reference) and 24 plan pins: the predicate reaches the outer scan as a single filter for `>` (also with a negative zero and under a null-safe correlation), `BETWEEN`, `IN` lists, a second correlated column, a correlated `IN` and a reference that is filtered already; it does not for `NOT EXISTS`, a mark that is output or under an `OR`, a plain scan on the left side, a function of the outer key, an `OR` or a NULL test on the key, the NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, a CTE with an unfiltered reference, and with the CTE filter pusher disabled. A last block repeats result cases with the CTE filter pusher disabled.

Existing tests: no expected plan or result changes. `test/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/join/*` and `test/sql/filter/*` pass, also with column binding verification, forced external operators, forced storage and forced row fetches.

This PR touches `cte_filter_pusher.cpp` in one place (the call of the helper) and adds one source file.

Relation to #28760 / #28639: those PRs change the filter dependency of delim CTEs in the other direction and remove identity projections around them; the plan pins of this test need to be re-run once they land. Relation to #28732: once `FILTER[mark](MARK)` is a SEMI join by the time the CTE filter pusher runs, the MARK check here is dead and can be removed; the SEMI case covers it.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent.

review_comments.body:
This absorption can remove rows a CTE consumer needs. `Expression::Equals` treats DOUBLE `0.0` and `-0.0` as equal, but `signbit` distinguishes them. If another reference’s conjuncts all match conjuncts here, the pusher drops this reference’s filter, even though implication doesn’t hold.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(k DOUBLE);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (-1), (1), (20);
WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM t)
SELECT k FROM c WHERE signbit(k * '0.0'::DOUBLE)
UNION ALL
SELECT k FROM c WHERE k > 10
UNION ALL
SELECT k FROM c WHERE signbit(k * '-0.0'::DOUBLE) AND k < 10
ORDER BY k;
```

This returns `-1, 20`; disabling `cte_filter_pusher` or using base `f467491ecae` returns `-1, 1, 20`. Disabling `semi_join_key_filter_transfer` leaves absorption enabled.

Could we compare the conjuncts by representation here (for example, constants with their exact value, sign of zero included), or skip the absorption when a conjunct contains a floating-point constant?

Fixed in 211a4133e17: the absorption in the CTE filter pusher now applies only to CTEs for which the new pass filtered a reference, and only when every conjunct of the reference that is kept compares a bare column with constants (comparison, BETWEEN, IN list, NULL test, AND/OR over those), so predicates such as `signbit(k * 0.0)` keep the disjunction; the repro returns -1, 1, 20 and is in the test.

Confirmed, the repro returns -1, 1, 20 on `211a4133e17`, and the targeted fuzz matches. Details are in the new review round.

The `CanThrow` bailout still needs coverage; this need not block. This case's left side is a scan, not a CTE reference, so it exits before `CanThrow`, as case 6 notes.

Pair these materialized CTE queries, asserting that `k < 4` reaches the CTE's scan of `fact` with the pusher on. In contrast, `k::UTINYINT < 4` is not transferred, and that query still returns `(1, 10), (1, 11), (2, 20), (3, 30), (3, 31)` without casting `-1`.

```sql
WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM fact)
SELECT * FROM c WHERE k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k::UTINYINT < 4) ORDER BY ALL;
WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM fact)
SELECT * FROM c WHERE k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k < 4) ORDER BY ALL;
```

+# name: test/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.test
+# description: The CTE filter pusher filters a materialized CTE on the left side of a SEMI join (or of a MARK join under a filter on its mark) by what the filters on the right side imply for the join keys: a correlated EXISTS with a predicate on the outer key only filters the outer scan
+# group: [optimizer]
+
+# fact: duplicate, NULL and unmatched keys (-1, 9); dim: duplicate and NULL keys, an unmatched key (7)
+statement ok
+CREATE TABLE fact(k INTEGER, v INTEGER);
+
+statement ok
+INSERT INTO fact VALUES (1, 10), (1, 11), (2, 20), (3, 30), (3, 31), (4, 40), (5, 50), (NULL, 60), (NULL, 61), (-1, 70), (9, 90);
+
+statement ok
+CREATE TABLE dim(k INTEGER, c INTEGER);
+
+statement ok
+INSERT INTO dim VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (3, 4), (4, 6), (5, 7), (NULL, 8), (7, 9);
+
+statement ok
+CREATE TABLE empty_dim(k INTEGER, c INTEGER);
+
+# 1: the outer-only conjunct of a correlated EXISTS: only fact rows with k > 2 can match
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+3	30
+3	31
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 2: the same with a predicate no row satisfies
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 100) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+
+# 3: NOT EXISTS keeps the rows that fail the predicate: nothing is transferred across an ANTI join / a NOT mark filter
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+-1	70
+1	10
+1	11
+2	20
+9	90
+NULL	60
+NULL	61
+
+# 4: EXISTS as a value: the mark is output, every fact row stays
+query III
+SELECT k, v, EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) AS e FROM fact f ORDER BY ALL
+----
+-1	70	false
+1	10	false
+1	11	false
+2	20	false
+3	30	true
+3	31	true
+4	40	true
+5	50	true
+9	90	false
+NULL	60	false
+NULL	61	false
+
+# 5: the mark under an OR is not a bare-mark filter
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) OR f.v = 10 ORDER BY ALL
+----
+1	10
+3	30
+3	31
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 6: an uncorrelated IN whose subquery filters its key (the left side is a scan, not a CTE reference: left alone)
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE f.k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k > 2) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+3	30
+3	31
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 7: BETWEEN
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE f.k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k BETWEEN 2 AND 4) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+2	20
+3	30
+3	31
+4	40
+
+# 8: an IN list
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE f.k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k IN (1, 3, 7)) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+1	10
+1	11
+3	30
+3	31
+
+# 9: an OR over the key
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE f.k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k < 2 OR k > 3) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+1	10
+1	11
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 10: a null-safe correlation: the NULL keys match each other
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM f.k AND f.k IS NULL) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+NULL	60
+NULL	61
+
+# 11: null-safe with an OR that keeps the NULL keys
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM f.k AND (f.k IS NULL OR f.k > 3)) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+4	40
+5	50
+NULL	60
+NULL	61
+
+# 12: a predicate on another column of the subquery says nothing about the key
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND d.c > 5) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 13: an outer-only conjunct on another outer column: every correlated column is a key of the join back
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.v > 25) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+3	30
+3	31
+4	40
+5	50
+
+# 14: an empty right side
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM empty_dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+
+# 15: an empty left side
+query II
+SELECT * FROM empty_dim f WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim d WHERE d.k = f.k AND f.k > 2) ORDER BY ALL
+----
+
+# 16: a predicate that can throw is not transferred: fact has k = -1, dim does not
+query II
+SELECT * FROM fact f WHERE f.k IN (SELECT k FROM dim WHERE k::UTINYINT < 4) ORDER BY ALL

title: Filter the outer scan of a correlated EXISTS by a predicate on the outer key only
